title: Ice-off temperature skill fell from 54% to 4% at a mean lead of 38 days with a monthly trend forecast
abstract: We tested whether published ice-off temperature relations keep their gain when future monthly temperature is unknown. We retained the published slopes and windows for 112 series and rebuilt 1509 test dates in 2005-2020. Median skill against a trailing ice-date mean was 0.538 with observed temperature. It was 0.039 with an expanding monthly trend forecast issued a mean 37.7 days before ice-off. Two climate-mean forecasts gave 0.049 and 0.057. Issue dates in the median ice-off month kept skill 0.482, but 30% followed the event. The observed-weather reconstruction matched source skill within 0.000006. An exact loss audit found that the climate-error cross term caused 19% of the mean loss at the 38-day lead. The test shows that a stable climate response does not alone establish useful lead-time skill. It tests simple climate forecasts, not archived numerical weather forecasts. It reuses the earlier test cohort and current data versions. Spatial dependence, record selection and data latency limit inference.

display.caption: Skill falls when recent temperature months are unknown. Intervals resample sites. Independent input-error limits are conditional diagnostics, not measured weather forecast errors.
